items.summary: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome Imran Bayoumi, Deputy Director & Resident Fellow at the Atlantic Council. He sees the Trump administration’s new sanctions strategy toward Iran as an attempt to seek economic leverage where military force has so far failed to produce any results. But its effectiveness rests on several unresolved assumptions. Iran, meanwhile, has decades of experience curtailing sanctions and is again threatening regional escalation.

items.title: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres offered on Monday to facilitate the transit of fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz which has been disrupted as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. “The purpose is simple: to reduce immediate risks, support more orderly and predictable transit and help rebuild the confidence necessary for diplomacy and de-escalation,” he said at a news conference. Guterres said the UN “would not authorise passage” through the strait or “alter the rights or obligations” of states under international law, but rather serve as a “neutral facilitator”, registering and verifying ships carrying fertiliser and related products. “Of course, it can only be done if the countries that are involved in this conflict all agree to accept the mechanism,” Guterres said, which would be coordinated by Oman.

items.title: US senator criticises economic 'D-Day' against Iran, says 'Trump is losing'
items.summary: US senator criticises economic 'D-Day' against Iran, says 'Trump is losing' US Senator Chris Murphy has criticised the White House’s new sanctions on Iran, warning that American citizens are "paying a huge, huge cost" for the decision. "'D-Day' is desperate window dressing. Iran is winning the war. Trump is losing. And Americans are paying a huge, huge cost," he said in a post on X. In a series of posts, Murphy went onto list a number of reasons for Washington's setbacks during its war on Iran, including not achieving initial war objectives, Tehran's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and the depletion of army resources, including its munition supply. "The bottom line: Trump lost the military campaign. And now he's desperate so in his humiliating defeat, he's selling this fake economic pressure to keep up the impression we are still fighting," the US senator added. "But the war is basically over. Tragically, Iran won. This is all window dressing." "D-Day" is desperate window dressing. Iran is winning the war. Trump is losing. And Americans are paying a huge, huge cost. 1/ Let'

items.summary: Iran president says time to end war while in position of strength Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday it was time to end the months-long war with the United States because Tehran appeared to be in a stronger position than Washington. Talks between the longtime foes remain on hold, and the war started by the US and Israel in February has been locked in a stalemate. Tehran is keeping the key Strait of Hormuz partially shut and Washington is persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran. "It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity," Pezeshkian said in a meeting with doctors. "The whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasises that America has attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all regulations and is hated around the world."

items.summary: Iran’s president calls for war to end ‘today’ from position of strength Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for an end to the war while Tehran remains “in a position of strength and dignity”, warning that Iran would crush any renewed attack. Pezeshkian described the negotiated agreement as a “major achievement” unanimously approved by Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. “They cannot find even one clause in this agreement that indicates surrender; all the commitments are on the other side,” the Iranian Students’ News Agency quoted him as saying. Pezeshkian said Iran should pursue peace without lowering its guard against possible deception. “We will under no circumstances bow to bullying,” he said. “We will stand against them until our last breath and give them a crushing response. “War has to end at some point. It is better to end the war today, while we are in a position of strength and dignity,” he added.

items.summary: China warns US of retaliation over expansion of Iran sanctions China on Tuesday warned the US that it could retaliate if Washington expands its sanctions campaign against Iran to target Chinese companies, potentially opening a new front in tensions between the world’s two largest economies. The warning came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced measures aimed at further isolating Iran and threatening countries that continue to trade with Tehran with exclusion from the dollar-based financial system. The Financial Times reported that Beijing had warned against any significant extension of secondary sanctions to Chinese businesses, with a foreign ministry spokesperson saying that China would take “all necessary measures” to protect its interests. items.summary: China warns US against expanding Iran sanctions to Chinese firms China has warned Washington that it will retaliate if the Trump administration significantly expands its Iran-related secondary sanctions against Chinese companies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced measures on Monday targeting companies in mainland China and Hong Kong. Washington stopped short of sanctioning major Chinese financial institutions. “China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests,” a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday. “China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” they said. “The pressing task is to facilitate de-escalation of the situation and return to dialogue and negotiation as soon as possible,” they added.

clusters.headline: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal

items.title: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal
items.summary: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran -backed Iraqi armed group, said on Saturday it will only cooperate with efforts to bring weapons under state control if 10 conditions are met, including a complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. The group said US forces must fully withdraw by land, sea and air, that any American presence “under any title” must end, and that Iraqi airspace must not be used to launch attacks on neighbouring countries. It also called for full federal control over Iraqi territory, stronger Iraqi-operated air defences with advanced systems, and the withdrawal of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) fighters and Turkish troops from northern Iraq. It said that the PKK's presence gives Turkey a pretext for cross-border operations. The group, which has longstanding ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), made its statement as the Iraqi government faces a 30 September deadline to bring all armed factions' weapons under state control.

items.title: El último bandazo de Trump en Irán depende de China
items.summary: En los últimos días y semanas, Trump y su Administración han obrado el último bandazo en la guerra contra el régimen de Teherán: una campaña económica que aísle todavía más a Irán de las finanzas globales y fuerce un acuerdo sobre su programa nuclear, el gran objetivo del presidente de EE.UU. El problema es que cumplir con ese plan tiene un problema: requiere de una confrontación directa con China, el gran sustento de Irán. Y Trump tendrá que hacer equilibrios entre lograr un verdadero aislamiento de Irán y no abrir un nuevo frente con Pekín.Trump y su secretario del Tesoro, Scott Bessent , han hablado de ello en las últimas semanas, en una indicación de su intención de dejar de lado -al menos, de momento- la presión militar y centrarse en la presión económica. Es el tercer giro del conflicto con Irán, que ha pasado de la guerra total a la ofensiva diplomática -sin gran éxito- y, ahora, a la presión económica. Una opción mucho más digerible que la militar para el votante estadounidense, también para el 'trumpismo', ahora que estamos a la vuelta de la esquina de las decisivas eleccion

items.title: Pakistani army chief discussed 'ending deadlock' in US-Iran talks during visit to Tehran
items.summary: Pakistani army chief discussed 'ending deadlock' in US-Iran talks during visit to Tehran Asim Munir, Pakistan's army commander, held "constructive consultations" on Monday with senior Iranian officials regarding regional peace and how to resolve escalating tensions, Iranian state media reported. The talks were held during Munir's one-day visit to Tehran as part of Islamabad's "diplomatic efforts to end the deadlock in US-Iran talks and explore ways to achieve lasting peace and a permanent end to instability in the region.", IRNA reported. Prominent Iranian figures that participated in the discussions included Masoud Pezhakian, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Mohsen Rezaee, Seyed Abbas Araghchi and Eskandar Momeni.

items.title: Pakistan army chief set to visit Tehran on Monday
items.summary: Pakistan army chief set to visit Tehran on Monday Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is set to visit Tehran on Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday. Baghaei said the visit was a continuation of Pakistan's efforts to strengthen peace and security in the region. This follows a phone call between Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in which the pair reportedly discussed the regional situation and ways to revive stalled ceasefire talks. In a post on X, Iran's foreign ministry said that the two discussed “regional developments and effective ways to strengthen peace, stability and security in West Asia". The discussions come amid a renewed push to revive talks by mediators Pakistan and Qatar.

items.title: Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plant
items.summary: Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down. The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. Continue reading...

items.title: Iranian hackers shut down UK power plant for four days, The Telegraph reports
items.summary: Iranian hackers shut down UK power plant for four days, The Telegraph reports Iranian hackers shut down a British power plant for four days in an unprecedented cyber attack, according to British newspaper The Telegraph. This is for the first time that Iranian hackers have succeeded in closing down such a facility in the UK, the newspaper reported. The attack, believed to be the most successful cyber attack of its kind, took place at the same time as a series of attacks on US water infrastructure last month, which affected 12 states and caused concern in the White House. The Telegraph said British officials did not reveal which power plant had been affected, citing security concerns, but it had learnt that it was a small plant. Although the outage had no impact on the UK’s wider power supply or energy generation, the UK government briefed the chief executives of power companies and wrote to businesses with advice, direction and next steps.

items.summary: This week, President Donald Trump formally submitted the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review, moving the deal forward despite continuing to insist that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel before it can take effect. This condition could stall the agreement indefinitely: Riyadh demands a clear pathway toward Palestinian statehood before normalization, and Israel is dead set against statehood. Israel had strongly opposed the deal as originally negotiated, while Netanyahu had privately expressed hopes of delivering “ the next big thing ” by securing Saudi normalization before Israel’s October elections. Former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney described Trump as inserting normalization “ at the last minute ,” throwing the agreement into uncertainty. Trump’s decision to submit the agreement for congressional review further adds to this uncertainty. The president appears to want it both ways: his latest move is signaling to Riyadh that the agreement is moving forward even as he assures Tel Aviv that the deal is contingent on normalization. items.summary: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions Long queues formed at petrol stations across Tehran on Tuesday after the United States announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran, AFP reported. The new measures come as Washington seeks to increase economic pressure on Tehran after six months of war that has reached a military stalemate, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz blocked. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday outlined plans for what he called the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, saying the objective was to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime”. According to AFP, Iranian authorities have largely shrugged off Washington’s threats, noting that the country has lived under US sanctions for decades. But residents in Tehran expressed concern that the latest measures could further affect fuel supplies and the wider economy. The queues at petrol stations came amid growing uncertainty over fuel availability and prices as the latest US measures add to economic pressure on Iran.

items.title: After 6 months of war, why aren't oil prices even higher?
items.summary: For decades, the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been considered the ultimate doomsday scenario for global oil markets. So, when Iran effectively closed the Strait earlier this year in response to the joint U.S.-Israeli assault, many analysts warned that oil prices could skyrocket to record highs. The logic was straightforward. Prior to the war, about 20% of the global oil supply transited the Strait. A loss of supply on this scale could easily have pushed oil prices to $150 or even $200 per barrel — but it didn’t. Instead, prices peaked around $120 per barrel in April and have largely stayed below $100 since June. To understand the dynamics that have so far prevented an even higher price spike, and to get a sense of where oil supply and prices may be headed as the conflict drags on, I spoke with Rory Johnston, a leading oil markets analyst and the author of the Commodity Context blog. items.title: UKMTO report says Hormuz traffic just 20 percent of pre-war levels
items.summary: UKMTO report says Hormuz traffic just 20 percent of pre-war levels Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to recover from the war, with new data showing traffic still running at roughly a fifth of pre-war volumes. Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) show 103 ships entered the strait and 89 left over the past week, which amounts to just 20 percent of the pre-war seven-day average. The curtailed traffic comes despite continued harassment from Iran's Revolutionary Guard, including drone overflights, VHF hailing of vessels, and active mine danger areas along the route. Tankers made up the bulk of the reduced traffic, accounting for 45 percent of all movements through the strait. UKMTO data also shows the southern Omani corridor has become the most dangerous stretch of the route, recording 16 of the 18 projectile strikes reported since 6 July. Tankers make up the bulk of the reduced traffic. (AFP)

items.summary: US sanctions 'declaration of war on all nations', Iran says Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, says new US sanctions against Iran amounted to a “declaration of war” on all countries and went beyond “an illegal economic war against a single nation”, according to Iran’s Fars news agency. Baghaei said: “The announcement of new sanctions represents an attempt by the United States to exert extraterritorial sovereignty over all independent UN member states.” “No government has the right to force foreign banks, enterprises, or airports, each operating under the exclusive jurisdiction of their own sovereignty, to refrain from engaging in legitimate trade with a third country.” The minister said “such secondary sanctions have no basis in international law” and “violated the fundamental principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article 2, Paragraph 1 of the UN Charter”. Baghaei warned that a surrender to “such intimidation would lead to the total erosion of national sovereignty” and serve as “a catastrophic return to blatant, full-scale colonialism”.

Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, as Lake America . items.title: Ghalibaf says 'no one will be able to sell oil in region where Iran can't'
items.summary: Ghalibaf says 'no one will be able to sell oil in region where Iran can't' Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has warned that “no one will be able to sell oil in a region where Tehran cannot”, according to Mehr News Agency. On Friday, Ghalibaf republished on X a message originally dated 22 July, responding to earlier claims by US Central Command (Centcom) commander Admiral Brad Cooper that American forces had achieved full control of the Strait of Hormuz and halted Iran's oil exports. “The equation of this war is clear: either all or none!” he said. “In a region where we don’t sell oil, no one else will sell oil either.” He also said that the security of the Strait of Hormuz, lies in “the absence” of US troops. “If our security is not ensured, no infrastructure will be safe,” he said, according to Mehr.

items.title: Iran will neither forgive nor forget Minab school massacre, Araghchi says
items.summary: Iran will neither forgive nor forget Minab school massacre, Araghchi says Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has said that his country will neither forgive nor forget the Minab school massacre “but will continue to pursue it”, IRNA reported. During a visit to the “Minab School” painting exhibition on Friday, Araghchi said human rights have “become a political tool in the hands of some Western states”, “exploiting them for political gain and attaching no real value to the concept”. “We believe in human rights in the true sense of the word in Iran and have always defended the rights of the Iranian people and will not allow it to be abused by others,” he added, according to IRNA. In February, a double strike on a girls' school in Minab in southern Iran killed 165 people, mostly students aged seven to 12. Local officials say about 170 girls were at the school during the attack, which Iran attributes to the US and Israel.

Banque Misr is Egypt's second-largest bank. Its Emirati arm will no longer be able to do business in US dollars as of 28 September, under the new plans. The 30-day notification period is open for public comment, a process whereby the US government solicits messages of support or opposition that could potentially sway the decision. "The US Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed a rule that would revoke Banque Misr UAE’s correspondent banking access to US financial institutions. Treasury assesses that Banque Misr UAE is a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to U.S. dollars," the Treasury said. clusters.headline: The Guardian climate pledge 2026

items.title: The Guardian climate pledge 2026
items.summary: Each year, the Guardian reaffirms its commitment to the environment – both in our reporting and how we operate as a business. From critical tipping points to war in Iran, this is how the last 12 months have looked Support the Guardian’s environment coverage The Guardian climate forum 2026 Today marks the end of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign. Each year, during the campaign, we remind our audience about the Guardian’s role in covering the threats to our planet and the importance of independent journalism in telling that story. items.title: The Guardian view on energy costs: vulnerable households need help with their bills | Editorial
items.summary: Soaring prices are plunging struggling families into debt. The government must support them in the short term as it invests in a clean energy future Fuelled by the consequences of Donald Trump’s disastrous war on Iran, household energy debt in Britain is continuing to soar, rising to a record £6bn by the end of June. That figure is set to hit £7bn by the end of the year, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices goes up to a three-year high in October. The human cost among the less well off will be more people regularly choosing whether to skip meals, ignore other bills or stay cold this winter. Such is life at the sharp end of the cost of living crisis, which Andy Burnham has made it his priority to address since arriving in Downing Street. The day after he became prime minister, Mr Burnham announced that VAT would be removed from electricity bills from the beginning of October. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him. Ihre Sicherheitsinteressen, so scheint es, werden beim Vorgehen der Trump-Regierung kaum berücksichtigt . Dennoch sprechen drei Gründe gegen ein Ende ihrer engen Bindung an Washington. "The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves its right to resort to all available means to pursue accountability, compensation and redress, and to hold the perpetrators of these inhumane and unlawful acts accountable," Araghchi said. He added that the US campaign "entails international responsibility, including an obligation to provide full compensation for all material and moral damages, including restitution and reparations, in accordance with international law". clusters.headline: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for saffron and tomato rice | A kitchen in Rome

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for saffron and tomato rice | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way … The saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way. Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics,

items.title: Trump's war and tariffs are having a nasty effect on interest rates
items.summary: Over the last month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has engaged in two controversial and rare interventions in financial markets. The first came in early August when the U.S. Treasury joined the government of Japan in its efforts to strengthen the yen by buying the Japanese currency, taking a step it had last taken during the Asian Financial Crisis in 1998. And late last week, Bessent announced that the Treasury could double the amount of long-dated Treasuries that it will buy back from current holders. The theme that unites both interventions is a concern that the interest rates the U.S government is paying on its long-term debt (also known as bond yields) are rising too high and too fast, with 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yields reaching 5.3%, levels last seen in 2007. Last February, Bessent said the administration was focused on lowering bond yields. items.summary: Iran’s nuclear chief says attacked nuclear sites not secure for IAEA inspection Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said on Wednesday that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would not be able to inspect the country's nuclear sites that have suffered attacks in recent months until it develops a specific inspection protocol for such sites and their security is ensured, adding that Iran is still in a wartime situation, in comments carried by Iran’s IRNA news agency. Eslami said that Trump's threats to bomb the alleged secret Iranian nuclear site show the IAEA are pawns of the US and Israel, and accused the countries of pressuring the IAEA for an inspection.

Le même jour, le président Massoud Pezeshkian a assuré que Washington n’obtiendrait « rien » par sa pression économique, tandis que Benjamin Netanyahu a exclu tout accord avec les dirigeants iraniens. L’armée iranienne a par ailleurs affirmé avoir « reconstruit » tous ses systèmes d’armes endommagés pendant la guerre.

items.title: Iran-Oman Hormuz agreement not yet finalised: Iranian source
items.summary: Iran-Oman Hormuz agreement not yet finalised: Iranian source Iran and Oman are still finalising an agreement on shares of the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, Reuters is reporting, citing a senior Iranian source. According to the source, the countries are still working on the details of the agreement. This comes shortly after Iranian media, citing an IRGC spokesman, reported that the two countries had "reached results that have been accepted by both sides". In comments carried by Tasnim news agency, the spokesman confirmed that: “Agreements have been reached on the share of each country in the waters of the strait and the share of Iran and Oman in its revenues."

Het vliegdekschip lag lange tijd in de Arabische Zee, waar het onder meer werd gebruikt voor de Amerikaanse luchtaanvallen op Iran. Het werd vorige week afgelost door een ander Amerikaans vliegdekschip, waardoor de Abraham Lincoln kon beginnen aan de terugreis naar de VS. According to the latest tallies Tuesday night, Graham, who was appointed to her brother’s seat after his death in July, beat her opponent Rep. Ralph Norman, 53% to 46% . It’s a curious turn of events in a modern era where there are very few displays of hereditary power, but she had the full backing of the Republican establishment and the fulsome endorsemen t of President Donald Trump days before today’s primary runoff. To be sure, her self-confessed lack of foreign policy experience or even knowledge won’t be a bad thing for Trump. Graham has all but said she will follow her brother’s career-long support of a militarized U.S. foreign policy, which means she is likely to be no critic of Trump’s failing war in the Middle East. items.summary: Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home Three moves in the last week have exposed the limits of Donald Trump’s economic bullying . The US slapped 50% tariffs on another $20bn of Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on the cars, trucks, parts and steel that America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs and pro-billionaire tax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasury stepped in to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it. items.summary: Het plan van de Verenigde Staten om Iran economisch te isoleren lijkt een "wanhoopsdaad", zegt VS-deskundige Philip Marey van Rabobank. Gisteravond presenteerde de Amerikaanse minister van Financiën Scott Bessent de uitbreiding van sancties tegen Iran als 'economische D-day '. En het blijft niet bij het economisch verstoten van Iran. Bessent dreigt ook met maatregelen tegen andere landen, bedrijven en personen die zakendoen met Teheran. Ook die kunnen gestraft worden. "Als je kijkt naar het verloop en de volgorde van de sancties, dan hadden de economische maatregelen ook eerder aangekondigd kunnen worden", zegt Marey. clusters.headline: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage

items.title: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage
items.summary: For decades, the United States treated the prospect of an Iranian nuclear weapon as an intolerable threat. Yet when Washington and Tehran went to war twice in roughly a year, America’s own nuclear arsenal provided remarkably little leverage. In June 2025, the United States joined Israel in attacking Iran’s nuclear facilities. Iran retaliated against Israeli territory and a U.S. air base in Qatar. The following year, a far larger U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and much of Iran’s senior military leadership while striking the country’s nuclear, military, energy, and transportation infrastructure. Tehran responded by attacking Israel, U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf, and regional energy infrastructure. In neither war did America’s overwhelming nuclear superiority prevent Iranian retaliation or compel Tehran to capitulate. The paradox is striking: the weapon the U.S. had long insisted Iran must never possess proved largely incapable of shaping Tehran’s calculations, or determining the course of a war of choice that has consumed Trump’s presidency. clusters.headline: Bessent admits sanctions may blow up global economy in apparent slip

items.title: Bessent admits sanctions may blow up global economy in apparent slip
items.summary: Bessent admits sanctions may blow up global economy in apparent slip US Treasury Secretary says that American sanctions on Iran could collapse the global economy, in an apparent slip while answering a question from a reporter at a press conference in Washington, DC to announce the santions. When asked by a reporter why the Treasury doesn't impose the sanctions today, Bessent replied "why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" He went on to elaborate that the US wants to give countries the "opportunity" to abide by their sanctions as a "warning shot" which, if ignored, will result in such nations being removed from the US dollar system. After he delivered the remarks, Bessent left the press conference, not taking any further questions. Bessent: "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" pic.twitter.com/vPXHtzS4IF — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) August 24, 2026

items.summary: Iranian and Pakistani top officials meet in Tehran Pakistan’s military chief Asim Munir met with Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in Tehran on Monday, according to Iran’s Mehr News Agency. The two discussed US violations of its commitments to implement the Pakistani-mediated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed with Iran in June. According to Mehr, Ghalibaf told Munir that “the US, by breaching its commitments, prevented the establishment of stability in the region and created another reason for distrust”. Munir said he will continue his efforts to restore stability in the region. items.summary: Israeli spy Jonathan Pollard wants Iran ‘off the map’, says wars on Turkey and Egypt are next Jonathan Pollard, the Israeli spy who betrayed the United States, has called on Israel to prepare for war against Egypt and Turkey as he launches his campaign for a Knesset seat in October’s election. The American-born former US Navy intelligence analyst spent 30 years in prison after passing a vast collection of classified documents to Israel. In an interview with Israeli news channel ILTV on Sunday, Pollard called on Israel to wipe Iran “off the map” and identified Egypt and Turkey as its next major enemies. “I hate to put it that way, but Turkey and Egypt are coming up next as our major strategic threat,” said Pollard. “And unless we have all these other fronts eliminated by that time, we're going to be in a terrible situation,” he added. Egypt and Turkey both maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, while Egypt signed a peace treaty with it in 1979. items.title: Houthis say they attacked vessel off Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Houthis say they attacked vessel off Saudi Arabia Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement said on Monday that it had attacked a vessel off the coast of Saudi Arabia near the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, made the statement in a televised speech. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment. Earlier on Monday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said a tanker had been struck by an unknown projectile about 63 nautical miles west of Yanbu. UKMTO said all crew members were safe and accounted for, with no reported environmental impact. Yanbu is Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil export port and has become an important route for Saudi crude shipments bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked amid the escalating confrontation with Iran.

They hardened it Submitted by Mahyar Ramezankhani on Fri, 08/21/2026 - 20:00 Tehran was denied a decade of growth, and given in exchange a tolerance for punishment that few open economies possess Iranian banknotes - households are paying the price (Atta Kenare/AFP) On The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed for most of the past six months. Brent crude is trading just below $90 a barrel, and rose about five percent in a single session earlier this month. Nieuwe boringen in Barentszzee zijn omstreden omdat de Europese Unie een verbod hierop steunt vanwege milieuoverwegingen. "In het huidige geopolitieke en veiligheidsklimaat, en gezien de situatie rondom de energievoorraden, geloof ik dat het voortzetten van de activiteiten in de Barentszzee zowel de Noorse als de Europese belangen dienen", zei Aasland tegen Reuters voorafgaand aan de energieconferentie ONS die maandag van start gaat. In 2022 spanden organisaties, waaronder Greenpeace, nog een rechtszaak aan tegen boringen in de Barentszzee. De eisers pleitten voor het terugdringen van emissies die klimaatverandering veroorzaken. De rechter van het Europees Hof voor de Rechten van de Mens oordeelde vorig jaar in het voordeel van de Noorse regering. items.summary: Senior in Iran's Basij says US was 'forced' to ask for ceasefire Hossein Taeb,  head of Iran's Basij paramilitary unit, remarked that that Tehran had not asked for a ceasefire, instead the US was "forced" to call for negotiations. "We reached a document through negotiations, but the other side could not tolerate this document for 60 days and violated it," Iranian media reported Taeb as saying. "They thought they could make this nation sit at home by returning to negotiations," he added. The senior Basij official also expressed that Iran's armed forces "stood firm" during the war and "exposed the weaknesses of the US military". "America put all its might into the field, thinking it could finish the job within three days to six weeks." Regarding the truce talks, Taeb said that Iran "did not weaken and ask for negotiations, but it was America that asked for negotiations".

items.title: Dozens of ex-lawmakers, staff landed at military firms since 2015
items.summary: In the last decade, 31 former members of Congress and top staff have left Capitol Hill and joined the military-industrial complex as lobbyists or contractors, according to a new report from the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The 21 lawmakers named in the report served on either the House or Senate Armed Services Committee, the legislative bodies that set the Pentagon’s annual policies through the annual National Defense Authorization Act. In addition, the report names 10 former senior committee staffers who transitioned to working as weapons industry government liaisons or lobbyists. These 31 former officials represent a snapshot of the military-industrial complex’s “revolving door,” through which ex-policymakers transition from setting the Pentagon’s agenda in Congress to cashing in on those same policies in the private sector. “That report we published is the most direct explanation we’ve ever seen of why the defense budget always goes up,” said John Mecklin, the author of the report and former editor-in-chief of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. clusters.headline: US can huff & puff, but without a political fix Iran won't come down

items.title: US can huff & puff, but without a political fix Iran won't come down
items.summary: The latest U.S. strategy in the Middle East is defined as one of “ maximum pressure ,” combining military containment and economic sanctions in an attempt to compel Iran to accept a deal. But it lacks clearly defined, civilian-led outcomes, illustrating the persistent misalignment between military means and political ends. Military pressure can set conditions, signal resolve, and buy time for civilian action. It cannot determine political outcomes. When a civilian-led strategy rooted in clear end states is not determined ahead of sending military forces, those deployments turn into continuous rotations; it is how ‘forever wars’ get started. This essay is not an argument against the use of force. It is at times necessary, and even realist restraint doctrine says so. Instead, this essay is an argument that force is but one of many instruments of national security; when the other instruments of national security, like diplomacy, aren’t employed equally or greater than the military, it is service members who pay the greatest price. The discussion between the two included “how countering Houthi lies and propaganda with timely, accurate facts is an important part of the battle," the US diplomat said. The Yemeni minister added that his country’s leadership now presents "a genuine opportunity" to deepen ties with the US and counter Houthi disinformation. Earlier on Sunday, the Yemeni government carried out drone attacks on Houthi targets across various locations, according to Yemeni government media.

items.title: Iranian parliamentary committee approves provision to charge ships in Hormuz
items.summary: Iranian parliamentary committee approves provision to charge ships in Hormuz Iranian parliament advanced a provision in a draft law on Sunday allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission approved Article 3 of its "Strategic Action to Ensure the Security and Progress of the Strait of Hormuz" plan, Iran's IRNA news agency reported. Based on the article, a fee will be charged for services "including maritime, environmental, fueling under special conditions, insurance, safety, and other services provided in the Strait of Hormuz." Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency. He added that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait. items.title: Pezeshkian says Iran’s 'power and cohesion had astonished the world'
items.summary: Pezeshkian says Iran’s 'power and cohesion had astonished the world' Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said that Iran was fighting a "full-scale economic, military and security war", but the nation's “power and cohesion had astonished the world". Speaking at a ceremony where participants renewed allegiance with the ideals of the Islamic Republic's founder, Pezeshkian said: "The enemies imagined that with their pressure and actions, Iran would collapse.” “Not only did this not happen, but the power and unity of the Iranian nation amazed the world," he said. Pezeshkian praised the people's resistance, saying analysts “could not easily explain how the nation had withstood such pressure”. "Our dear people truly performed a miracle," he said, according to the Mehr news agency. "Of course, we are ashamed before the people that problems exist," Pezeshkian said, "but as long as we have breath in our bodies, we will serve our dear people and pass through these crises with strength."

items.title: US set to remove Syria from 'sponsors of terrorism' list
items.summary: US set to remove Syria from 'sponsors of terrorism' list Syria is set to be removed from the US State Sponsors of Terrorism list after nearly 47 years. A mandatory 45-day congressional review period expired on 22 August without reported action to block the move. The remaining step is formal publication of the rescission in the Federal Register by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Washington designated Syria a state sponsor of terrorism on 29 December 1979, citing support for international terrorism under then-President Hafez al-Assad. The designation remained through Bashar al-Assad’s rule and the Syrian civil war. President Donald Trump notified Congress on 8 July that his administration intended to rescind the designation, saying Syria’s government had not supported international terrorism during the previous six months and had pledged not to do so. The move follows the collapse of the Assad government in December 2024 and Washington’s effort to reset ties with Syria’s transitional authorities. items.title: Georgia declines to join new EU sanctions against Iran
items.summary: Georgia declines to join new EU sanctions against Iran Georgia has declined to join the European Union’s latest sanctions against Iran, saying its foreign policy decisions are guided by national interests, Iran’s state news agency, IRNA, reported. Tengiz Sharmanashvili, a representative of Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party in parliament, said Tbilisi decides whether to back international measures based on whether they serve Georgia’s interests at a particular time. “If a decision conflicts with Georgia’s interests, it simply does not matter to us whose interests it serves,” he said, according to IRNA. Sharmanashvili also pointed to Turkey and Serbia, saying neither country had joined the latest EU sanctions despite their status as EU candidates.

clusters.headline: Israel has no intention of escalating tensions with Turkey, foreign minister says

items.title: Israel has no intention of escalating tensions with Turkey, foreign minister says
items.summary: Israel has no intention of escalating tensions with Turkey, foreign minister says Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said on Saturday that Israel does not seek escalation with Turkey, but "will not accept" Turkish presence in Syria. "We are committed to preserving the status quo ... We will not accept the establishment of Turkish bases in Syria," Saar told Israeli news outlet Channel 12 in an interview. He said Israel has observed how Iran "infiltrated" Lebanon and Gaza, adding: "We don't want that same situation with Turkey and Syria." Saar's remarks followed recent Israeli strikes on Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase, which Israel says were carried out based on intelligence suggesting Turkey was planning to deploy troops there. Both Syria and Turkey have rejected claims that there were such plans to establish a permanent Turkish military presence in Syria.

His remarks came after US President Donald Trump announced new sanctions against Tehran, describing the move as "the most crushing economic operation” against Iran.

items.title: How China eased pressure on oil markets by halting purchases and relying on reserves
items.summary: How China eased pressure on oil markets by halting purchases and relying on reserves The closure of the Strait of Hormuz should, in principle, have caused a far greater shock to oil markets than it has. This, in large part, is due to China’s policy of using its strategic stockpiles rather than purchasing crude oil at inflated prices due to the war. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day (bpd) – a fifth of global daily oil consumption – with an estimated 10 to 14 percent of global supply remaining inaccessible six months on. Even so, it has not had the same repercussions as previous comparable Middle East crises. The 1973 Arab oil embargo, which quadrupled prices, disrupted only seven percent of global supply, while both the 1979 Iranian revolution and 1990 invasion of Kuwait more than doubled prices, each blocking only six to seven percent. In comparison, current oil prices have risen by “only” around 50 percent, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, stabilising near $85-90 a barrel, up from around $60 at the start of the year. items.summary: Iran says its armed forces emerged stronger from latest war Iran’s acting Defence Minister Seyed Majid Ebn al-Reza says Tehran will resist any attack on the country’s territory, independence or security. Addressing worshippers before Friday prayers in Tehran, Ebn al-Reza said Iran entered the “Ramadan War” significantly stronger than during the earlier 12-day conflict, state broadcaster IRIB reported. He described the war as a “harsh test” that inflicted deaths and heavy losses but strengthened national confidence. “This war showed that the Iranian nation can withstand all threats if it stands on its own feet, trusts its youth, puts science and technology at the forefront, and remains united,” he said. Ebn al-Reza said Iran had sharpened its ability to penetrate “enemy bases, monitor regional movements and inflict heavier losses”, while developing more advanced tactics and technology. “Iran’s defence power today is not for warmongering, but to prevent war and aggression,” he said. “We have never initiated aggression against any country, and we never will,” he added.

items.title: Iranian oil prices rise as US blockade tightens supplies to China
items.summary: Iranian oil prices rise as US blockade tightens supplies to China Iranian crude prices have climbed as fewer cargoes reach Chinese buyers under a tightening US blockade, Reuters reports. Traders said Iranian oil deliveries for September and October had fallen below volumes in July and August. Sellers have already placed much of the crude shipped earlier, leaving fewer barrels available. Iranian oil that traders offered at discounts is now commanding premiums as supplies tighten. The shift follows a decline in Iranian exports since mid-July, when the United States intensified its blockade on the country’s oil shipments. Pressure on buyers could increase after US President Donald Trump threatened secondary sanctions on Thursday against countries that continue trading with Iran. China remains the largest destination for Iranian crude despite years of US sanctions.

clusters.headline: Iran parliament chief visits graves of allied Iraqi fighters

items.title: Iran parliament chief visits graves of allied Iraqi fighters
items.summary: Iran parliament chief visits graves of allied Iraqi fighters Iran’s parliament speaker has paid tribute to Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis during a visit to Iraq, according to Iran’s Student News Network. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf visited al-Muhandis’s grave at Wadi al-Salam cemetery in the Iraqi city of Najaf on the third day of a trip by an Iranian parliamentary delegation. The speaker also visited the burial sites of other members of Iran-backed Iraqi armed groups, the network reported. Al-Muhandis served as deputy commander of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella organisation of armed groups established during the fight against ISIL. A US drone strike killed him and Iran’s general, Qassem Soleimani, near Baghdad International Airport in January 2020.

items.summary: The Trump-connected Polymarket is likely helping gamblers with inside military information cash in on wars the president wages. According to the non-profit research group, these wallets had a 97.2% success rate and won $8 million collectively. Moreover, Trump Jr. and his brother, Eric Trump, continue to profit from defense industry investments as the war with Iran continues. items.summary: US vows to 'collapse' Iran with new sanctions as energy prices spike The US will impose "the toughest sanctions in history” on Iran, Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Thursday, vowing to ramp up economic pressure on the Islamic Republic even as the economic toll of the war builds. "It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade [on Iran], and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history," Bessent told CNBC. "It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime,” he said, adding that the sanctions will be explained on Monday. Bessent’s statements come a day after Trump said that he was launching an "economic D-Day" on Iran, and warned that any country helping Tehran would face "TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences". items.summary: La guerra de Irán ha provocado la mayor crisis de suministro de la historia del petróleo. Ni siquiera en los momentos más intensos de los combates los precios del petróleo alcanzaron los 150 dólares por barril que muchos analistas habían pronosticado al inicio del conflicto. Esto se lo debemos agradecer a algunos gobiernos. Poco después de que las municiones iraníes hicieran intransitable el estrecho de Ormuz, dejando atrapados 14 millones de barriles al día de crudo en el Golfo, los monarcas petroleros de Abu Dabi y Riad desviaron 5 millones de barriles al día adicionales a través de oleoductos que eludían el estrecho. Los ministros de Washington y Tokio liberaron una cantidad récord de 2 millones de barriles al día de reservas de emergencia; el racionamiento impuesto por el Estado en los países más pobres redujo considerablemente la demanda.Sin embargo, la catástrofe se habría producido de todos modos sin las decisiones tomadas discretamente en otra capital: Pekín. As commanders review readiness across key fronts, Yemen’s political leadership is signaling that attacks will no longer be absorbed without a response. Together, the developments suggest that the country’s long period of “no war, no peace” may be coming to an end. There has been no ground offensive large enough to redraw the map so far. But war can return gradually as long-range strikes increase, forces reinforce positions and the rules of retaliation begin to change. items.title: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal
items.summary: Iran-backed Iraqi group sets 10 conditions for disarmament, including full US withdrawal Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran -backed Iraqi armed group, said on Saturday it will only cooperate with efforts to bring weapons under state control if 10 conditions are met, including a complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. The group said US forces must fully withdraw by land, sea and air, that any American presence “under any title” must end, and that Iraqi airspace must not be used to launch attacks on neighbouring countries. It also called for full federal control over Iraqi territory, stronger Iraqi-operated air defences with advanced systems, and the withdrawal of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) fighters and Turkish troops from northern Iraq. It said that the PKK's presence gives Turkey a pretext for cross-border operations. The group, which has longstanding ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), made its statement as the Iraqi government faces a 30 September deadline to bring all armed factions' weapons under state control.

items.title: The rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract us | Arwa Mahdawi

Or Natalie Harp. Or “affordability”, which, as Donald Trump recently said at a rally, is a word that was “never used” by the media before he took office. Best not to talk about anything that affects ordinary people or embarrasses the president, really. Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, as Lake America . On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to America-fy the lake’s name on US maps and documents, which is an excellent use of time and resources. I suppose we can at least be thankful that the president, who is trying to slap his own name on everything from airports to the Kennedy Center , didn’t decree that the body of water be called Lake Trump. items.summary: This week, President Donald Trump formally submitted the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review, moving the deal forward despite continuing to insist that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel before it can take effect. This condition could stall the agreement indefinitely: Riyadh demands a clear pathway toward Palestinian statehood before normalization, and Israel is dead set against statehood. Israel had strongly opposed the deal as originally negotiated, while Netanyahu had privately expressed hopes of delivering “ the next big thing ” by securing Saudi normalization before Israel’s October elections. Former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney described Trump as inserting normalization “ at the last minute ,” throwing the agreement into uncertainty. Trump’s decision to submit the agreement for congressional review further adds to this uncertainty. The president appears to want it both ways: his latest move is signaling to Riyadh that the agreement is moving forward even as he assures Tel Aviv that the deal is contingent on normalization. "We are at the beginning of a long and sustainable road defined by dignity, revival, reconstruction, development and civilisation," Sharaa said during the opening of the 63rd Damascus International Fair. The head of the UN Agency for Palestinian Refugees (Unrwa) told Al Jazeera that the Israeli government’s raid on the last remaining facility run by the UN agency earlier this weep is an attempt to "eliminate the presence of the United Nations" in the occupied Palestinian territories. items.summary: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way … The saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way. Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics,

De bemanning vertrok in november vorig jaar. Doel was een missie van vier à vijf maanden op de Stille Oceaan, maar toen de oorlog tegen Iran eind februari begon, vertrok het schip naar het Midden-Oosten. Het vliegdekschip lag lange tijd in de Arabische Zee, waar het onder meer werd gebruikt voor de Amerikaanse luchtaanvallen op Iran. Het werd vorige week afgelost door een ander Amerikaans vliegdekschip, waardoor de Abraham Lincoln kon beginnen aan de terugreis naar de VS. In their essay, which was the basis of the book of the same name that appeared the next year, Mearsheimer and Walt had been careful to distinguish the Israel lobby from a lobby by and for Jews, but it was to no avail in the furor that the essay and book provoked. items.title: El último bandazo de Trump en Irán depende de China
items.summary: En los últimos días y semanas, Trump y su Administración han obrado el último bandazo en la guerra contra el régimen de Teherán: una campaña económica que aísle todavía más a Irán de las finanzas globales y fuerce un acuerdo sobre su programa nuclear, el gran objetivo del presidente de EE.UU. El problema es que cumplir con ese plan tiene un problema: requiere de una confrontación directa con China, el gran sustento de Irán. Y Trump tendrá que hacer equilibrios entre lograr un verdadero aislamiento de Irán y no abrir un nuevo frente con Pekín.Trump y su secretario del Tesoro, Scott Bessent , han hablado de ello en las últimas semanas, en una indicación de su intención de dejar de lado -al menos, de momento- la presión militar y centrarse en la presión económica. Es el tercer giro del conflicto con Irán, que ha pasado de la guerra total a la ofensiva diplomática -sin gran éxito- y, ahora, a la presión económica. The US slapped 50% tariffs on another $20bn of Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on the cars, trucks, parts and steel that America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs and pro-billionaire tax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasury stepped in to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it. items.title: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions
items.summary: Iranians queue for petrol after US announces new sanctions Long queues formed at petrol stations across Tehran on Tuesday after the United States announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran, AFP reported. The new measures come as Washington seeks to increase economic pressure on Tehran after six months of war that has reached a military stalemate, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz blocked. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday outlined plans for what he called the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, saying the objective was to “sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime”. According to AFP, Iranian authorities have largely shrugged off Washington’s threats, noting that the country has lived under US sanctions for decades. But residents in Tehran expressed concern that the latest measures could further affect fuel supplies and the wider economy. The queues at petrol stations came amid growing uncertainty over fuel availability and prices as the latest US measures add to economic pressure on Iran.

items.title: US economic D-Day sanctions: 'Repeated bombing attacks across Iran failed to change the calculus'
items.summary: Genie Godula is pleased to welcome Imran Bayoumi, Deputy Director & Resident Fellow at the Atlantic Council. He sees the Trump administration’s new sanctions strategy toward Iran as an attempt to seek economic leverage where military force has so far failed to produce any results. But its effectiveness rests on several unresolved assumptions. Chief among them is whether Washington can compel China, Iran’s largest oil customer, to comply despite Beijing’s growing economic resilience. Iran, meanwhile, has decades of experience curtailing sanctions and is again threatening regional escalation.

Bessent se negó a identificar a los países afectados o a revelar cuándo entrarían en vigor las sanciones, indicando que, en cambio, les daría tiempo para cumplir con la nueva directiva. De twee schepen gisteren waren een grote gastanker en een grote olietanker. Waardoor het aantal schepen zo sterk is gedaald, is niet duidelijk. Wellicht waren het er meer dan twee, omdat sommige schepen hun navigatiesystemen uitschakelen tijdens de passage. Iran heeft ondertussen 45 tankers op een zwarte lijst gezet wegens vermeende overtreding van Iraanse regels voor het varen door de zeestraat. Het land dreigt ook met maatregelen tegen schepen die goederen overslaan naar of van deze tankers. Voor het uitbreken van het conflict in de regio ging ongeveer een vijfde van de wereldwijde olie en aardgas door de Straat van Hormuz. items.title: After 6 months of war, why aren't oil prices even higher?
items.summary: For decades, the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been considered the ultimate doomsday scenario for global oil markets. So, when Iran effectively closed the Strait earlier this year in response to the joint U.S.-Israeli assault, many analysts warned that oil prices could skyrocket to record highs. The logic was straightforward. Prior to the war, about 20% of the global oil supply transited the Strait. A loss of supply on this scale could easily have pushed oil prices to $150 or even $200 per barrel — but it didn’t. Instead, prices peaked around $120 per barrel in April and have largely stayed below $100 since June. To understand the dynamics that have so far prevented an even higher price spike, and to get a sense of where oil supply and prices may be headed as the conflict drags on, I spoke with Rory Johnston, a leading oil markets analyst and the author of the Commodity Context blog. items.title: Turns out having nukes provided the US very little leverage
items.summary: For decades, the United States treated the prospect of an Iranian nuclear weapon as an intolerable threat. Yet when Washington and Tehran went to war twice in roughly a year, America’s own nuclear arsenal provided remarkably little leverage. In June 2025, the United States joined Israel in attacking Iran’s nuclear facilities. Iran retaliated against Israeli territory and a U.S. air base in Qatar. The following year, a far larger U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and much of Iran’s senior military leadership while striking the country’s nuclear, military, energy, and transportation infrastructure. Tehran responded by attacking Israel, U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf, and regional energy infrastructure. In neither war did America’s overwhelming nuclear superiority prevent Iranian retaliation or compel Tehran to capitulate. The paradox is striking: the weapon the U.S. had long insisted Iran must never possess proved largely incapable of shaping Tehran’s calculations, or determining the course of a war of choice that has consumed Trump’s presidency. items.title: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: UN offers to facilitate fertiliser transit through Strait of Hormuz UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres offered on Monday to facilitate the transit of fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz which has been disrupted as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. “The purpose is simple: to reduce immediate risks, support more orderly and predictable transit and help rebuild the confidence necessary for diplomacy and de-escalation,” he said at a news conference. Guterres said the UN “would not authorise passage” through the strait or “alter the rights or obligations” of states under international law, but rather serve as a “neutral facilitator”, registering and verifying ships carrying fertiliser and related products. “Of course, it can only be done if the countries that are involved in this conflict all agree to accept the mechanism,” Guterres said, which would be coordinated by Oman.

items.summary: Hegseth says US not ruling out military force against Iran US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that President Donald Trump's administration was not ruling out using further military force against Iran, even as Washington unveiled an "economic D-Day" of new sanctions against Tehran. "By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran," Hegseth told reporters, adding that Iran could not handle the economic pressure it was under. Meanwhile, Iran's economy minister has claimed that the country has a "two-year plan" to deal with the sanctions and that the US will suffer "another defeat" as a result.

items.title: Bessent admits sanctions may blow up global economy in apparent slip
items.summary: Bessent admits sanctions may blow up global economy in apparent slip US Treasury Secretary says that American sanctions on Iran could collapse the global economy, in an apparent slip while answering a question from a reporter at a press conference in Washington, DC to announce the santions. When asked by a reporter why the Treasury doesn't impose the sanctions today, Bessent replied "why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" He went on to elaborate that the US wants to give countries the "opportunity" to abide by their sanctions as a "warning shot" which, if ignored, will result in such nations being removed from the US dollar system. After he delivered the remarks, Bessent left the press conference, not taking any further questions. The American-born former US Navy intelligence analyst spent 30 years in prison after passing a vast collection of classified documents to Israel. Egypt and Turkey both maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, while Egypt signed a peace treaty with it in 1979. The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, made the statement in a televised speech. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment. Earlier on Monday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said a tanker had been struck by an unknown projectile about 63 nautical miles west of Yanbu. UKMTO said all crew members were safe and accounted for, with no reported environmental impact. Yanbu is Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil export port and has become an important route for Saudi crude shipments bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked amid the escalating confrontation with Iran.

items.title: Senior in Iran's Basij says US was 'forced' to ask for ceasefire

"We reached a document through negotiations, but the other side could not tolerate this document for 60 days and violated it," Iranian media reported Taeb as saying. "They thought they could make this nation sit at home by returning to negotiations," he added. The senior Basij official also expressed that Iran's armed forces "stood firm" during the war and "exposed the weaknesses of the US military". "America put all its might into the field, thinking it could finish the job within three days to six weeks." Regarding the truce talks, Taeb said that Iran "did not weaken and ask for negotiations, but it was America that asked for negotiations".

items.summary: In the last decade, 31 former members of Congress and top staff have left Capitol Hill and joined the military-industrial complex as lobbyists or contractors, according to a new report from the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The 21 lawmakers named in the report served on either the House or Senate Armed Services Committee, the legislative bodies that set the Pentagon’s annual policies through the annual National Defense Authorization Act. items.title: US can huff & puff, but without a political fix Iran won't come down
items.summary: The latest U.S. strategy in the Middle East is defined as one of “ maximum pressure ,” combining military containment and economic sanctions in an attempt to compel Iran to accept a deal. But it lacks clearly defined, civilian-led outcomes, illustrating the persistent misalignment between military means and political ends. Military pressure can set conditions, signal resolve, and buy time for civilian action. It cannot determine political outcomes. When a civilian-led strategy rooted in clear end states is not determined ahead of sending military forces, those deployments turn into continuous rotations; it is how ‘forever wars’ get started. This essay is not an argument against the use of force. It is at times necessary, and even realist restraint doctrine says so. Instead, this essay is an argument that force is but one of many instruments of national security; when the other instruments of national security, like diplomacy, aren’t employed equally or greater than the military, it is service members who pay the greatest price. items.title: Yemen, US officials meet to discuss ‘countering Houthi propaganda’
items.summary: Yemen, US officials meet to discuss ‘countering Houthi propaganda’ Yemen's Minister of Information Moammar al-Eryani and the US Embassy's chargé d'affaires in Yemen, Neal H. Opdahl, met on Sunday, according to a post on X by the US Embassy in Yemen. The discussion between the two included “how countering Houthi lies and propaganda with timely, accurate facts is an important part of the battle," the US diplomat said. The Yemeni minister added that his country’s leadership now presents "a genuine opportunity" to deepen ties with the US and counter Houthi disinformation. The meeting came as the Iran-backed Houthis continue to strike ships in the Red Sea. Earlier on Sunday, the Yemeni government carried out drone attacks on Houthi targets across various locations, according to Yemeni government media.

items.title: Iranian parliamentary committee approves provision to charge ships in Hormuz
items.summary: Iranian parliamentary committee approves provision to charge ships in Hormuz Iranian parliament advanced a provision in a draft law on Sunday allowing Tehran to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission approved Article 3 of its "Strategic Action to Ensure the Security and Progress of the Strait of Hormuz" plan, Iran's IRNA news agency reported. Based on the article, a fee will be charged for services "including maritime, environmental, fueling under special conditions, insurance, safety, and other services provided in the Strait of Hormuz." Committee spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said the fees would be collected from vessels belonging to countries permitted to pass through the strait and paid in Iranian rials or another currency. He added that the draft legislation takes into account the rights of states bordering the Strait. items.summary: Iran executes man charged with aiding US, Israel in January protests Iran on Sunday executed a man accused of carrying a chainsaw during January anti-government protests, who was charged with acting as an agent of Israel and the United States. The judiciary said Majid Adineh had been convicted of "operational action in favour of hostile groups" in nationwide rallies that broke out late last year. Adineh was accused of "deliberate arson, gathering and collusion with the intention of committing crimes against the country's internal security", the judiciary's Mizan Online website said in a report on Sunday. "Based on numerous documents and evidence in the case and the defendant's statements, the Karaj Revolutionary Court sentenced him to death and confiscation of all his property." An appeal by Adineh was unsuccessful, and the supreme court upheld the verdict, with his execution carried out Sunday morning, Mizan said. Reporting by AFP

items.summary: Iranian hackers shut down UK power plant for four days, The Telegraph reports Iranian hackers shut down a British power plant for four days in an unprecedented cyber attack, according to British newspaper The Telegraph. This is for the first time that Iranian hackers have succeeded in closing down such a facility in the UK, the newspaper reported. The attack, believed to be the most successful cyber attack of its kind, took place at the same time as a series of attacks on US water infrastructure last month, which affected 12 states and caused concern in the White House. The Telegraph said British officials did not reveal which power plant had been affected, citing security concerns, but it had learnt that it was a small plant. Although the outage had no impact on the UK’s wider power supply or energy generation, the UK government briefed the chief executives of power companies and wrote to businesses with advice, direction and next steps.

items.summary: Six EU countries urge windfall tax on energy firms as profits soar due to Iran war Six European Countries are stepping up calls for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies as profits soar due to the Middle East war, according to a letter seen by AFP. A mandatory 45-day congressional review period expired on 22 August without reported action to block the move. The remaining step is formal publication of the rescission in the Federal Register by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Washington designated Syria a state sponsor of terrorism on 29 December 1979, citing support for international terrorism under then-President Hafez al-Assad. The designation remained through Bashar al-Assad’s rule and the Syrian civil war. President Donald Trump notified Congress on 8 July that his administration intended to rescind the designation, saying Syria’s government had not supported international terrorism during the previous six months and had pledged not to do so. items.title: US sanctions 'declaration of war on all nations', Iran says
items.summary: US sanctions 'declaration of war on all nations', Iran says Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, says new US sanctions against Iran amounted to a “declaration of war” on all countries and went beyond “an illegal economic war against a single nation”, according to Iran’s Fars news agency. Baghaei said: “The announcement of new sanctions represents an attempt by the United States to exert extraterritorial sovereignty over all independent UN member states.” “No government has the right to force foreign banks, enterprises, or airports, each operating under the exclusive jurisdiction of their own sovereignty, to refrain from engaging in legitimate trade with a third country.” The minister said “such secondary sanctions have no basis in international law” and “violated the fundamental principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article 2, Paragraph 1 of the UN Charter”. Baghaei warned that a surrender to “such intimidation would lead to the total erosion of national sovereignty” and serve as “a catastrophic return to blatant, full-scale colonialism”.

items.title: UKMTO report says Hormuz traffic just 20 percent of pre-war levels
items.summary: UKMTO report says Hormuz traffic just 20 percent of pre-war levels Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to recover from the war, with new data showing traffic still running at roughly a fifth of pre-war volumes. Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) show 103 ships entered the strait and 89 left over the past week, which amounts to just 20 percent of the pre-war seven-day average. The curtailed traffic comes despite continued harassment from Iran's Revolutionary Guard, including drone overflights, VHF hailing of vessels, and active mine danger areas along the route. Tankers made up the bulk of the reduced traffic, accounting for 45 percent of all movements through the strait. UKMTO data also shows the southern Omani corridor has become the most dangerous stretch of the route, recording 16 of the 18 projectile strikes reported since 6 July. Tankers make up the bulk of the reduced traffic. (AFP)

Addressing a rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, Trump said: “We cannot let them have a nuclear weapon, we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or you will see some very bad things.” “They want to make a deal so badly, we don’t even know if we want [a deal] because I view the Strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now, it’s an American territory,” Trump said, according to Al Jazeera.

items.title: Georgia declines to join new EU sanctions against Iran
items.summary: Georgia declines to join new EU sanctions against Iran Georgia has declined to join the European Union’s latest sanctions against Iran, saying its foreign policy decisions are guided by national interests, Iran’s state news agency, IRNA, reported. Tengiz Sharmanashvili, a representative of Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party in parliament, said Tbilisi decides whether to back international measures based on whether they serve Georgia’s interests at a particular time. “If a decision conflicts with Georgia’s interests, it simply does not matter to us whose interests it serves,” he said, according to IRNA. Sharmanashvili also pointed to Turkey and Serbia, saying neither country had joined the latest EU sanctions despite their status as EU candidates.

items.title: Iran president says time to end war while in position of strength
items.summary: Iran president says time to end war while in position of strength Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday it was time to end the months-long war with the United States because Tehran appeared to be in a stronger position than Washington. Talks between the longtime foes remain on hold, and the war started by the US and Israel in February has been locked in a stalemate. Tehran is keeping the key Strait of Hormuz partially shut and Washington is persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran. "It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity," Pezeshkian said in a meeting with doctors. "The whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasises that America has attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all regulations and is hated around the world."

In a letter published in The Nation, Iranian academic Maryam Tahmasebi described the arrest and detention of her husband, Eissa Hashemi, their 16-year-old son and herself, as "bloodline punishment" as the three permanent residents were stripped of their green cards following an online campaign. items.title: How China eased pressure on oil markets by halting purchases and relying on reserves
items.summary: How China eased pressure on oil markets by halting purchases and relying on reserves The closure of the Strait of Hormuz should, in principle, have caused a far greater shock to oil markets than it has. This, in large part, is due to China’s policy of using its strategic stockpiles rather than purchasing crude oil at inflated prices due to the war. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day (bpd) – a fifth of global daily oil consumption – with an estimated 10 to 14 percent of global supply remaining inaccessible six months on. Even so, it has not had the same repercussions as previous comparable Middle East crises. The 1973 Arab oil embargo, which quadrupled prices, disrupted only seven percent of global supply, while both the 1979 Iranian revolution and 1990 invasion of Kuwait more than doubled prices, each blocking only six to seven percent. In comparison, current oil prices have risen by “only” around 50 percent, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, stabilising near $85-90 a barrel, up from around $60 at the start of the year.
